title: Tourists in Our Own Backyard
summary: A writer, a professor, and an overdue mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge in Concord. Our photographs and watercolors, local history, a map, and practical access notes.
search: Concord, Massachusetts · Time for two Tourists in Our Own Backyard A mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge. A writer, a professor, three years living nearby—and a little literary pilgrimage we somehow hadn’t made. Our photographs, watercolors, local history, and the practical details for a visit of your own. October 21, 2026 · An AUsome Life Louisa May Alcott’s resting place, from our own visit to Authors’ Ridge. I’m a writer. Dad is a professor. We’d lived here for three years.And somehow, we had never made the trek to Authors’ Ridge. On paper, we were very well qualified to have done this already. But a funny thing happens when you live near somewhere people travel to see: it becomes the place you can visit any time. And “any time” has a way of slipping behind everything that actually has a date on the calendar. So, for a little while this fall, we became tourists in our own backyard. Our date took us to Authors’ Ridge in Concord’s Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, where Louisa May Alcott, Henry David Thoreau, Nathaniel Hawthorne and Ralph Waldo Emerson are buried. Familiar names, suddenly attached to very small, very human places. About the writers and the cemetery. The things people leave behind Look closely at the photographs. Around Louisa May Alcott’s marker are pencils, pinecones, stones and a pink rose. At Thoreau’s, more pencils lie among the roots and needles, beneath a little stone that simply says Henry. I find the pencils especially moving. Such ordinary things, brought to the graves of people whose words have lasted so long. To me, they look like small thank-yous: your work reached someone. Someone is still reading. Hawthorne’s marker has its own quiet simplicity. A rounded stone, a surname, sunlight and shadow. You can know a name for years and still feel differently about it when you stand in front of it, outdoors, at the scale of a person. Henry: a small marker, tree roots, and the things visitors have left. Hawthorne, in patches of sun and shade. In our photographs, the trees still hold plenty of green. A little gold is beginning to show. The ground has its own autumn palette: brown needles, gray stone, moss, a bright flower. There is enough to look at before you read a single name. Before the graves, there were evening walks One of my favorite pieces of this place’s history is that the writers knew it as a place to walk. The National Park Service records that Emerson, Thoreau, and Nathaniel and Sophia Hawthorne enjoyed evening walks in Sleepy Hollow before it became a cemetery. Before these woods held their graves, they held their evening walks. That makes a date here feel part of a much older habit: going outside together, looking around, letting a familiar landscape give you something to think about. Sleepy Hollow was dedicated on September 29, 1855, with an address by Emerson. Landscape architects Horace William Shaler Cleveland and Robert Morris Copeland planned paths and drives around the natural shape of the land, respecting its trees and plants. The Concord Free Public Library’s dedication exhibit describes that approach—and notes that the place already carried the name Sleepy Hollow before it was a burial ground. It belongs to the nineteenth-century tradition of rural or garden cemeteries, where landscape and remembrance meet. The winding roads and wooded setting are part of the history you have come to see. Read about the landscape. A little more of the neighborhood Concord’s history reaches much further back than the writers. The Concord Museum identifies the area as the original homelands of the Nipmuc, Massachusett and Pawtucket tribal nations, and recognizes Indigenous people’s continuing connection to this land. Nearby, the North Bridge holds another chapter: the battle of April 19, 1775. A visit to Concord can open onto many histories. Authors’ Ridge gave us plenty to notice on its own. Something lovely, close to home A date like this makes room for the people we are as well as the people we look after. I’m still a writer. Dad is still someone who loves ideas. And we are still two people who can go somewhere together and find things worth noticing. I like that the visit didn’t need to be elaborate to be worth remembering. A nearby place, a little curiosity, a few photographs. There is a particular pleasure in finally doing the thing that has been waiting so close to home. Three years was a long time to get around to it. I’m glad we finally went. From the photographsA little autumn sketchbook Three watercolor interpretations of our visit. title: Old friends, an autumn wedding & a weekend away.
summary: An autumn wedding in New Haven, old college friends from Bristol and Rome, a little time away, and the grandparents who made it possible.
search: From the autumn camera roll · New Haven, Connecticut Old friends, an autumn wedding & a weekend away. College friends from Bristol and Rome, a wonderful wedding, a downtown hotel, and a little time to ourselves. A November 2018 memory · Shared October 22, 2026 All dressed up for a lovely autumn weekend. I've been loving all the old autumn photos that keep resurfacing on my phone lately. Every few days, another little memory pops up — a place we visited, people we love, or a wonderful weekend I'd nearly forgotten about. And these photographs from November 2018 took me right back to New Haven, Connecticut. We were there to celebrate the wedding of our dear friends Deb and Artur, and it was such a lovely excuse to reconnect with college friends from my years in Bristol, Rhode Island, and Rome, Italy. ❤️ There are some friendships that will always remind you of a particular time in your life — the places you went, the adventures you had, and the person you were back then. Seeing everyone again was such a treat. A sweet New England wedding detail, right down to the date on the maple-leaf bottle. A weekend away takes a village. Of course, leaving James for a weekend is never particularly easy for me. As many parents and caregivers know, even the loveliest getaway comes with a fair amount of planning (and perhaps a little worrying!). Thankfully, James was in wonderful hands with Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve, who love him beyond measure and have always been such an important part of our village. Knowing he was with people who know and adore him made it easier to enjoy a little grown-up time. ❤️ We stayed at the beautiful Omni New Haven Hotel at Yale, right downtown. It was such a treat to enjoy a lovely hotel, explore New Haven in autumn, catch up with old friends, and have a little time away from our everyday routines. And the New Haven pizza? Oh, my goodness. 🍕 That's a whole 'nother delicious story, and one that absolutely deserves its own post! Old friends, dressed for the occasion. A heartfelt family remembrance among the wedding details. Dessert, with a side of disco lighting. There may have been some spectacular fashion choices. And yes, the novelty hats came out. 😂 The people are the best part. Deb and Artur's wedding was beautiful, with heartfelt family tributes, wonderful food, lots of laughter, and some truly spectacular fashion choices once the novelty hats and oversized sunglasses made their appearance. But I think what I loved most was simply being together again. There is something so special about friendships that stretch across years, countries, and completely different chapters of life. The people who knew you when you were young and figuring everything out, and who still feel like old friends no matter how much time has passed. And as much as I love sharing adventures with James, these occasional grown-up getaways are part of our story, too. Being a caregiver is a huge part of my life, but so are the friendships, places, memories, and experiences that have helped make me who I am. One more thing worth rememberingGood people make room for good weekends. This getaway was possible because Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve could be there for James. That kind of trusted family support matters, and I never take it for granted. Not every family has it; it's one reason I believe time for caregivers, and real support to make it possible, is so important. I'm so glad these photos found their way back onto my phone this autumn. A lovely reminder of a beautiful weekend, two wonderful people, and friendships I'm very grateful to have made along the way. ❤️ Here's to Deb and Artur, old friends, and all the stories that follow us home. 🍁 Explore related topics Places & outings Travel & stays

title: A little Easter color.
summary: An Easter family visit to Berlin Farms in Massachusetts: colorful eggs, an enthusiastic bunny, wide-open fields and a few practical notes before you go.

White fences beyond the buildings. One orange jacket that had apparently declined the pastel dress code.Our Easter photographs from Berlin Farms deserved a little space in the journal. Opened from the family albumThe eggs were everywhere.There is a particular sort of New England spring photograph: green beginning to return to the grass, bare trees in the distance, and everybody sensibly still wearing a jacket. Our Berlin Farms pictures have all of that, with the addition of a lawn covered in pink, yellow, blue and green eggs.A canvas shopping bag is ready for the egg hunt. The Easter Bunny has a pink bow, a floral backdrop, and considerably more enthusiasm for posing than most adults can sustain. I especially like the photograph with the arms up. There is plenty happening in it, and that smile is the part I keep coming back to.Then there is the family picture: the three of us together, the bunny at one end, and the stone patio beneath our feet. I am glad we have that one. A canvas tote, a lawn full of eggs, and a very visible orange jacket.All of us in the frame. The bunny makes four. A little spring color. Original editorial illustration.Between the photographsA little room to look around.The farm makes a lovely setting for this chapter. White clapboard buildings sit beside lines of white fencing, with fields stretching beyond them. In one photograph, a horse is grazing in the distance. The colors are mostly green, white and gray, which leaves the orange jacket with very little competition.I like having a wider view among the close-ups. It brings back the shape of a place: the deck, the fence, the buildings around the egg-hunt lawn. A family album needs a little of the scenery, too. White fences, open fields, and a sky still considering its spring options. One for the albumThe good part is right here.The photographs beside the black door are worth keeping in the set. There is a cap being adjusted, a yellow egg on the grass, and four very large letters spelling LOVE. The farm has helpfully supplied the caption.A tote bag, a bunny, and a few photographs I am glad we took.That is what I want to keep from this Easter visit: the color on the lawn, the bunny pictures, and our family together in the middle of it.One more photograph beside the LOVE door. title: A little Bristol blue.
summary: A family photograph from Bristol, Rhode Island, a short waterfront guide, and our experience practicing staying together safely.
search: The journalBristol, Rhode IslandFrom the family archives · October 19, 2026 An afternoon by the harborA little Bristol blue.Sailboats, stripes, and a much smaller James. A photograph from the family album, with a short guide for an afternoon on the waterfront.Looking through old photos and found this one. Apparently, we all got the memo about wearing blue.The three of us by the water. From an earlier family visit. Glad we took this one.Bristol, Rhode Island: sailboats, sparkling water, and a family afternoon by the harbor. There is James in front, with the boats behind us and the sun on the water.There is a practical detail in the photograph, too. James and I were each holding a voluntary walking handle as we practiced staying together safely. Nothing was attached to him; there was no tether or restraint, and he could let go at any time.For our family, it was one way to practice while getting out and enjoying the community. Every child and family has different needs, and what worked for us may not feel right or be appropriate for someone else. It was one small part of our experience, alongside close supervision.Mostly, I am glad we have this picture. An afternoon by the water with my two favorite people. Original editorial illustration, inspired by Bristol. An imagined harbor scene, separate from our family photograph. A small plan for a day outAlong the waterfront.These are researched ideas for a visit today, rather than a list of places we visited on the afternoon in our photograph.Start at Independence Park.At 419–459 Thames Street, this four-acre park overlooks Bristol Harbor and marks the southern end of the East Bay Bike Path. The state tourism listing includes walkways and public restrooms; check restroom availability for your visit. A good starting point for watching the boats without committing to a long walk.Independence Park visitor informationTake a waterfront wander.The town points visitors to the boardwalk behind Stone Harbour condominiums, leading toward Rockwell Park and the Maritime Center. Choose a short stretch, stop for the view, and turn back whenever you like.Bristol’s official places guideTry a little of the bike path.The East Bay Bike Path runs 13.8 miles between Providence and Bristol. You do not have to tackle the whole thing: a short out-and-back from Independence Park can be enough. Cyclists share the path, so plan the support and space your family needs.East Bay Bike Path detailsMake Audubon a separate stop.The Audubon Nature Center and Aquarium at 1401 Hope Street has exhibits, walking trails and a boardwalk toward Narragansett Bay. Audubon describes its facility and trails as accessible. Check opening hours, admission and closure announcements before heading over.Audubon visitor informationBefore you go: check parking signs, restroom access and waterfront conditions. Bristol announced funding for seawall work at Independence Park and the Maritime Center in October 2026; the notice does not establish a closure schedule, so check local updates before visiting. Waterfront routes can include open edges, docks and boat activity.Official visitor sources checked October 19, 2026. This is a family recollection with a researched guide, not a current accessibility audit. Town seawall project notice. About the walking handle & practicing staying together safelyWe each held part of the handle, with James choosing to hold his. It gave us a way to practice walking together. Unexpected separation can become dangerous quickly, even with attentive caregivers.A similar style is called Hold-On Handles. This link shows the type of product, not a confirmed match for ours; current stock and suitability need checking.In a 2012 parent survey involving 1,218 autistic children, 49% were reported to have attempted elopement at least once after age four. That describes the surveyed group, not any individual child’s future. Read the original study in Pediatrics.The practical, hopeful part is making room for learning and finding supports that fit. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends teaching safety skills alongside consistent adult supervision and an individual safety plan. Read the AAP’s guidance for families.A voluntarily held handle can be released at any moment. It cannot prevent unexpected separation or replace close supervision, particularly near water or traffic. We are sharing our experience, not general advice or a recommendation for restraint. Neither source establishes that a walking handle reduces elopement.Different people need different supports. For us, the point was getting out together and having opportunities to practice. Share this storySend a little Bristol to someone.Know someone who would enjoy an afternoon by the harbor?
